symptoms.title: Yellowing leaves
symptoms.description: Leaves are turning yellow, pale or lime green.

options.label: Mostly the older, lower leaves
The new growth at the top
Leaves all over the plant

questions.text: How does the soil feel right now?

options.label: Wet or soggy, maybe a musty smell
Bone dry and pulling from the pot edges
Slightly moist, nothing unusual

causes.title: Overwatering
causes.explanation: Constantly wet soil starves the roots of oxygen and can lead to root rot, which shows up first as yellow, soft leaves.
signs: Yellow lower leaves that feel soft or limp
Soil stays wet for days
Musty smell or black, mushy roots
Fungus gnats around the pot
remedies: Stop watering and let the top 2-3 inches of soil dry out before watering again.
Check that the pot has drainage holes and empty the saucer after every watering.
If the soil smells bad, slide the plant out, trim black or mushy roots and repot in fresh, well-draining mix.
Move the plant to brighter indirect light so the soil dries faster.
Use a moisture check with your finger before every watering instead of a fixed schedule.

causes.title: Underwatering
causes.explanation: When the roots run out of water the plant sacrifices leaves, which turn yellow, then dry and crispy.
signs: Yellow leaves that feel dry or papery
Soil is hard and shrunken away from the pot
Pot feels very light
Leaves drop easily
remedies: Water slowly and thoroughly until it drains out of the bottom of the pot.
If water runs straight through, bottom-soak the pot in a tub for 20-30 minutes.
Remove fully yellow or crispy leaves so the plant can focus on healthy growth.
Set a reminder in Bloomie to water on a consistent schedule.

causes.title: Nutrient deficiency
causes.explanation: A shortage of nitrogen, iron or magnesium causes pale or yellowing leaves, often with the veins staying green.
signs: Pale or uniformly light green leaves
Slow or stunted growth
Yellowing between green veins
Plant has not been fed or repotted in over a year
remedies: Feed with a balanced liquid houseplant fertilizer at half strength every 4 weeks in spring and summer.
Repot into fresh potting mix if the soil is old and compacted.
Flush the soil with plain water every few months to remove fertilizer salts.
Skip fertilizer in winter when growth slows.

causes.title: Natural leaf aging
causes.explanation: Plants regularly shed their oldest leaves as new growth emerges. A single yellow lower leaf now and then is normal.
signs: Only one or two of the oldest leaves are yellow
New growth looks healthy
No other symptoms
remedies: Gently pull or snip off the yellow leaf at the base.
Keep your current watering and light routine.
Keep an eye out: if more leaves follow quickly, recheck watering and light.

causes.title: Water quality or minerals
causes.explanation: Hard tap water with lots of minerals, chlorine or fluoride can build up in the soil and cause pale, yellow-tinged leaves.
signs: White crust on the soil or pot rim
Pale new leaves
Leaf tips burn or yellow over time
remedies: Switch to filtered, rain or distilled water, or let tap water sit out overnight before use.
Flush the soil thoroughly with plain water to wash out mineral buildup.
Repot into fresh soil if the crust returns quickly.

symptoms.prevention: Check the soil with your finger before every watering, use a pot with drainage and feed lightly during the growing season.

symptoms.title: Brown, crispy tips
symptoms.description: The tips or edges of the leaves are turning brown and dry.

questions.text: How is the air around your plant?

options.label: Dry: heating, air conditioning or a very dry room
Normal indoor air
Hot and sunny, right at a window

questions.text: What do the damaged areas look like?

options.label: Thin dry brown tips and edges
Brown tips plus a white crust on the soil
Large bleached or brown patches in the middle of leaves

causes.title: Low humidity
causes.explanation: Tropical plants lose moisture faster than their roots can supply it in dry air, so the leaf tips dry out first.
signs: Dry brown tips on several leaves
Worse in winter when heating is on
Leaf edges curl inward
Common on calatheas, ferns and peace lilies
remedies: Group plants together to create a more humid microclimate.
Run a humidifier nearby or set the pot on a pebble tray with water below the pebbles.
Keep the plant away from heaters, radiators and air-conditioning vents.
Trim brown tips with clean scissors, following the natural leaf shape.

causes.title: Minerals and chemicals in tap water
causes.explanation: Salts, chlorine and fluoride accumulate in the soil and are pulled into the leaf tips, where they burn the tissue.
signs: Crispy brown tips on a plant that otherwise looks healthy
White or yellow crust on the soil surface
Problem returns after trimming
remedies: Switch to distilled, filtered or rain water.
Flush the soil by watering heavily and letting it drain freely every month or two.
Scrape off the crust on the soil surface and top up with fresh potting mix.
Trim damaged tips for appearance.

causes.title: Underwatering
causes.explanation: If the soil dries out completely too often, the plant cannot supply the furthest leaf tips with water.
signs: Soil is dry deep down
Leaves feel thin and papery
Brown tips with drooping leaves
remedies: Water until it drains from the bottom, then empty the saucer.
Bottom-soak very dry pots for 20-30 minutes.
Water on a consistent schedule and check the soil weekly.

causes.title: Inconsistent watering
causes.explanation: Swinging between bone dry and soggy stresses the roots, and the damage appears at the leaf tips.
signs: Brown tips and some yellowing together
Watering is irregular
Soil is sometimes soggy, sometimes parched
remedies: Pick a routine and stick with it, checking the soil before you water.
Use Bloomie's reminders so watering is spaced evenly.
Choose a pot size that fits the root ball, since too large a pot stays wet too long.

causes.title: Fertilizer burn
causes.explanation: Too much fertilizer builds up salts in the soil that scorch the roots and leaf tips.
signs: Brown tips soon after feeding
White crust on soil or pot
Wilting even when the soil is moist
remedies: Flush the soil with plenty of plain water, letting it drain completely.
Pause fertilizer for 6-8 weeks.
When you resume, dilute to half the recommended strength.

causes.title: Sun scorch
causes.explanation: Direct midday sun burns the leaf tissue, leaving crispy brown or bleached patches.
signs: Bleached or brown patches facing the window
Damage on the sunniest side only
Leaves feel hot and dry
remedies: Move the plant a few feet back from the window or add a sheer curtain.
Trim badly burned leaves. They will not recover.
Reintroduce stronger light gradually over a couple of weeks if the plant needs it.

symptoms.prevention: Use filtered water, keep the humidity up for tropical plants and avoid sudden shifts in watering or location.

symptoms.title: Drooping or wilting
symptoms.description: The whole plant or its stems look limp, saggy or floppy.

questions.text: Push a finger 2 inches into the soil. How does it feel?

options.label: Dry and crumbly
Wet or soggy
Evenly moist
I repotted or moved the plant
It is near a heater, a cold window or a draft
Nothing has changed

causes.title: Thirst
causes.explanation: Without enough water the plant loses the internal pressure that holds leaves and stems upright, so it droops.
signs: Dry soil and a light pot
Leaves droop but are not yellow or mushy
Plant perks up within hours of watering
remedies: Water deeply until water runs out of the drainage holes.
For very dry soil, soak the pot in a basin of water for 20-30 minutes.
Check back in a few hours. A thirsty plant usually recovers quickly.
Set a Bloomie reminder to avoid repeating the cycle.

causes.title: Overwatering and root rot
causes.explanation: Waterlogged soil suffocates the roots. Damaged roots cannot take up water, so the plant wilts even though the soil is wet.
signs: Wet soil and drooping leaves together
Yellowing leaves and soft stems at the base
Dark, mushy roots with a bad smell
remedies: Do not water again. Move the plant to a bright spot with good airflow.
Slide it out of the pot and cut away any black, mushy or smelly roots.
Repot into fresh, well-draining mix in a pot with drainage holes.
Water lightly for the first few weeks while new roots form.

causes.title: Root-bound plant
causes.explanation: When the pot is full of roots there is little soil to hold water, so the plant dries out quickly and wilts.
signs: Roots circling or poking out of the drainage holes
Water runs straight through the pot
Plant dries out within a day or two
remedies: Repot into a container 1-2 inches wider with fresh potting mix.
Loosen the outer roots gently before planting.
Water well after repotting and keep it out of direct sun for a week.

causes.title: Heat or cold stress
causes.explanation: Hot, dry air or a sudden cold draft makes the plant lose water faster than it can take it up.
signs: Droop near a heater, vent or cold window
Leaves feel cold or curl
Sudden change after a season shift
remedies: Move the plant away from heaters, radiators, air conditioners and drafty windows.
Aim for a steady 18-25°C (65-77°F) for most houseplants.
Mist or add a humidifier if the air is hot and dry.

causes.title: Transplant shock
causes.explanation: Repotting or moving a plant disturbs the roots and its environment, causing a temporary droop while it adjusts.
signs: Droop starting a day or two after repotting or moving
Soil is moist and healthy
No pests or spots
remedies: Be patient and keep conditions steady for 2-3 weeks.
Avoid fertilizer until you see new growth.
Keep the plant in bright indirect light and water only when the top inch is dry.

symptoms.prevention: Check the soil by touch before watering, repot when roots fill the pot and keep plants away from extreme temperatures.

symptoms.title: Pale or leggy growth
symptoms.description: The plant is stretching, thin, pale, or growing small leaves far apart.

questions.text: How much light does the plant get?

options.label: A dim room or far from any window
A bright spot with plenty of daylight
It leans strongly toward the window

questions.text: When did you last fertilize or repot?

options.label: More than a year ago, or never
In the last few months
It is winter and growth has slowed

causes.title: Not enough light
causes.explanation: Plants stretch toward light by growing long, weak stems with widely spaced, smaller, paler leaves. This is called etiolation.
signs: Long gaps between leaves
Small, pale leaves
Leaning toward the window
Variegation fading to plain green
remedies: Move the plant closer to a bright window with filtered light.
In dark homes add a full-spectrum grow light for 8-12 hours a day.
Prune leggy stems to encourage bushier growth. Stretched stems will not shorten by themselves.
Make light changes gradually to avoid shocking the plant.

causes.title: Uneven light
causes.explanation: If light only reaches one side, the plant grows lopsided and leans toward the source.
signs: Plant bends toward the window
Dense growth on one side and sparse growth on the other
remedies: Rotate the pot a quarter turn every week.
Place the plant where light reaches it from more than one direction.

causes.title: Lack of nutrients
causes.explanation: Without nutrients in the soil, new growth comes in pale and weak even when light is good.
signs: Pale green or yellowish new leaves
Slow growth in the growing season
No fertilizer for over a year
remedies: Feed with a balanced liquid fertilizer at half strength every 4 weeks in spring and summer.
Refresh the top few inches of soil or repot with fresh mix.
Do not fertilize in winter when growth is naturally slow.

causes.title: Needs pruning
causes.explanation: Vining and branching plants grow long and sparse unless you pinch or prune them regularly.
signs: Long bare stems with leaves only at the tips
Few side shoots
remedies: Cut stems back just above a node using clean scissors.
Root the cuttings in water or soil to make new plants and fill out the pot.
Pinch growing tips regularly to encourage branching.

causes.title: Root-bound
causes.explanation: When roots have filled the pot the plant cannot absorb enough water and nutrients, which slows and thins the growth.
signs: Roots circling the inside of the pot or coming out of drainage holes
Water drains immediately
Growth has stalled
remedies: Repot into a container 1-2 inches larger with fresh potting mix.
Loosen the outer roots and trim any that are dead or circling tightly.
Water well and keep out of direct sun for a week.

symptoms.prevention: Place plants where they get bright indirect light, rotate them weekly and feed lightly in the growing season.

symptoms.title: Pests or spots
symptoms.description: You see bugs, webbing, sticky residue, or spots and patches on the leaves.

options.label: Fine webbing and tiny speckles on leaves
White cottony fluff on stems or leaf joints
Tiny black flies around the soil
Brown or black spots with yellow rings
Sticky leaves or small brown bumps
Warm and dry air
Soil stays wet or the room is humid
I recently brought home a new plant

causes.title: Spider mites
causes.explanation: Tiny sap-sucking mites thrive in warm, dry air and cause stippled leaves that eventually turn yellow and drop.
signs: Fine silky webs between leaves and stems
Tiny yellow or white speckles on leaves
Leaves turn dull and bronze
remedies: Isolate the plant from the others right away.
Rinse the plant thoroughly in the shower, especially the underside of the leaves.
Spray with insecticidal soap or neem oil solution every 5-7 days for 3-4 weeks.
Raise humidity, since mites dislike moist air.
Remove heavily infested leaves and discard them.

causes.title: Mealybugs
causes.explanation: Soft white insects that hide in cottony clusters and feed on plant sap, weakening the plant and leaving sticky honeydew.
signs: White cottony fluff in leaf joints and under leaves
Sticky residue on leaves
Distorted or stunted new growth
remedies: Isolate the plant immediately.
Dab each visible bug with a cotton swab dipped in 70% isopropyl alcohol.
Spray the whole plant with insecticidal soap or neem oil weekly for at least a month.
Check the soil and roots, since mealybugs can also live there.
Inspect nearby plants closely for spread.

causes.title: Fungus gnats
causes.explanation: Small flies that breed in constantly moist soil. The adults are an annoyance but the larvae can nibble delicate roots.
signs: Tiny black flies hovering around the plant or soil
Soil stays wet for long periods
Flies run across the soil surface
remedies: Let the top 2 inches of soil dry out fully between waterings.
Place yellow sticky traps near the soil to catch adults.
Treat the soil with a mosquito-bit (BTI) solution to kill the larvae.
Top the soil with a layer of sand or fine gravel to deter egg-laying.

causes.title: Fungal or bacterial leaf spot
causes.explanation: Water sitting on leaves and poor airflow let fungi and bacteria infect leaf tissue, producing spreading spots.
signs: Brown or black spots with yellow halos
Spots that grow or merge
Leaves that stay wet overnight
remedies: Remove and discard affected leaves with clean scissors.
Water at the soil level and avoid wetting the foliage.
Improve airflow and space the plants out.
Treat with a copper-based or houseplant fungicide if the spots keep spreading.

causes.title: Scale insects
causes.explanation: Small armored bugs that attach to stems and leaf undersides, feeding on sap and leaving sticky honeydew.
signs: Small brown or tan bumps on stems and leaves that scrape off
Sticky leaves
Sooty black mold on the honeydew
remedies: Isolate the plant and scrape off visible scale with a soft brush or fingernail.
Wipe stems and leaves with alcohol-soaked cotton swabs.
Apply neem oil or horticultural oil every 7-10 days for a month.
Wipe away sticky honeydew with a damp cloth.

causes.title: Aphids
causes.explanation: Soft-bodied green, black or brown insects that cluster on tender new growth and suck plant sap.
signs: Clusters of small insects on new shoots and buds
Sticky honeydew on leaves
Curled or distorted new leaves
remedies: Spray them off with a strong stream of water or wipe them away by hand.
Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil every 5-7 days until they are gone.
Isolate the plant until you have seen no aphids for two weeks.

symptoms.prevention: Inspect new plants and quarantine them for two weeks, check the undersides of leaves weekly and avoid keeping soil constantly wet.
